items.content_text:
Public Works is adding crews to close the gap on brush collection. Starting Friday, more dedicated brush trucks are on the road, and crews are running 10-hour days, six days a week.
 3 things that speed up your street: 
 1)  Keep piles at the yard's edge and clear of parked vehicles
 2) Keep materials in separate piles. Brush, bulk trash, bagged yard waste, and leaves each get picked up by a different specialized truck — a mixed pile often gets skipped.
 3) Dispose of smaller piles in regular garbage receptacles, if possible.
 Can't wait? Brush can be dropped off the Wood Recycle Center and bulk trash can go to any city refuse center, both free of charge.
 Thanks for your patience!

items.content_text:
When we choose a location for a new tree, we focus on neighborhoods that experience higher temperatures and have less access to shade. Our goal is to bring the benefits trees provide to the places that need them most.
 Once we identify the right place to plant, we decide on the right tree. While we do provide ongoing care for our trees, we also want to make sure the species we select has what it needs to thrive.
 Many of our trees face extreme heat, weed eaters, wind, and much more. We do our best to choose diverse, native species that are well-suited to their environment and give them the best chance of survival.
 Be sure to check out the short documentary about Chattanooga Tree Project, courtesy of Time:Stamp.

Preserve Chattanooga is proud to be an active member of the National Preservation Partners Network, connecting our work in Chattanooga with preservation leaders and organizations across the country. This September, NPPN will bring that network together in Washington, DC, for important conversations about advocacy, preservation policy, easements, housing, and the future of historic preservation.
Preservationists from Across the Country to Convene in Washington, DC
 National Preservation Partners Network hosts its 2026 Fall Convening and National Preservation Easement Summit, September 24–26
 KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — The National Preservation Partners Network (NPPN) will bring historic preservation leaders, advocates, and preservation easement professionals from across the country to Washington, DC, this September for two connected events: the 2026 Fall Convening and the 2026 National Preservation Easement Summit, taking place September 24–26 at the First Congregational United Church of Christ, 945 G Street NW.
 Both gatherings are presented in conjunction with the National Trust for Historic Preservation’s National Preservation Summit, giving attendees the rare opportunity to advocate, learn, and network alongside hundreds of fellow preservationists in the nation’s capital during a single trip.
 Fall Convening: Advocacy Meets Community:
 The Fall Convening opens Thursday, September 24, with a full day of advocacy on Capitol Hill, presented in partnership with the National Trust for Historic Preservation and Preservation Action. Attendees will meet directly with members of Congress and their staff to advocate for historic preservation as essential for American communities, supported by briefings, talking points, and guidance from the National Trust’s Government Relations team. The day concludes with a joint reception on Capitol Hill.
 On Friday, September 25, programming shifts to First Congregational United Church of Christ for a full day of sessions developed by NPPN members and led by leaders from across the field, including:
 ● Hot Topics in Preservation Law, including Section 106, with Cultural Heritage Partners
 ● Membership & Annual Giving Campaigns with Barbara O’Reilly of Windmill Hill Consulting
 ● Preservation’s Role in Solving the Housing Crisis, a panel with Donovan Rypkema of PlaceEconomics and Lauren McHale of The L’Enfant Trust
 ● Local Advocacy Programs with Rebecca Miller of the DC Preservation League
 ● A spotlight on the African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund with Nakita Reed
 ● A tour of the recently renovated Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library, a 1972 Mies van der Rohe building
 A guided walking tour of Lafayette Square — including Lafayette Park, the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, the recently renovated St. John’s Church, Decatur House, and The Octagon — will be offered Saturday, September 26, hosted by Washington Walks.
 National Preservation Easement Summit: Specialized Training for Easement Professionals:
 Running alongside the Fall Convening, the National Preservation Easement Summit brings together colleagues from organizations that hold and manage preservation easements — or are looking to start an easement program — for two full days of specialized programming, September 24–25. Made possible through the generous sponsorship of GBX Group, the Summit connects attendees with national experts and peers on topics including:
 ● The latest proposed legislation affecting preservation easements, straight from the Hill
 ● Funding and marketing an easement program
 ● Best practices for managing easement portfolios and handling violations
 ● Baseline documentation and data management
 ● An Easement Roundtable for attendees to bring challenges to discuss with peers
 ● 3-Minute Success Stories and visits to local easement-protected properties
 Summit attendees will also join the Thursday evening reception on Capitol Hill and the Friday evening meet-up, and are welcome to join the optional Saturday tour of Lafayette Square.
 Registration
 Early Bird pricing for each event is available through September 11: $250 for NPPN members and $300 for non-members. After September 11, pricing increases to $300 for members and $350 for non-members. Attendees are responsible for their own accommodations; the venue is within easy walking distance of the Metro Center and Chinatown/Gallery Place Metro stops.
 Learn more about both events here: https://prespartners.org/retreats/
 Register online at weblink.donorperfect.com/NPPNFall2026.
 About the National Preservation Partners Network
 The National Preservation Partners Network (NPPN) connects local, regional, statewide and national preservation organizations across the country, helping members learn from one another, adapt proven tools to new contexts, and build collaborative capacity for impact at the local, regional, and national levels. Connected for what’s next in preservation, NPPN is headquartered in Knoxville, Tennessee.

 National Preservation Partners Network

 www.prespartners.org

By 2060, Italy’s working-age population is projected to shrink by nearly 35%, one of the largest declines in the OECD. 
 But low salaries and poor-quality jobs discourage young Italians from entering the workforce or cause them to emigrate. High-school graduates struggle to find work.  
 What needs to change?  
 The #OECD Economic Survey of Italy recommends:  
 ➡️Expanding the network of Istituti Tecnici Superiori (ITS) technical schools to better align skills with employers’ needs  
 ➡️Encouraging on-the-job training and high-quality internships to ease the transition from school to work  
 ➡️Lowering the tax wedge for low-income workers Learn more by downloading the 2026 Economic Survey of Italy

 Passing a stopped school bus when the red lights are flashing and the stop arm is extended is against the law. Drivers in both directions are required to stop, except when the roadway is divided by a physical median, such as a concrete barrier or grass divider.
 Violating this law in Tennessee can lead to a fine and add 8 points to your driver's license

People who grow up in families that own their home are much more likely to become homeowners as adults.
 As owning a home has traditionally been a key pathway to building wealth, the decline in homeownership also risks widening wealth gaps over generations and between homeowners and renters.
 OECD analysis explores recent trends in household wealth and highlights significant wealth gaps across different demographic groups. It also reveals potential impacts for equal opportunity for future generations and examines policy action needed to reverse the trend.
 Following #InternationalYouthDay, explore one of the major challenges affecting young people’s financial futures: https://brnw.ch/21x4WO9 | #OECDyouth

Domestic violence doesn’t always leave bruises—but it can still be deadly. 😔
 In No Visible Bruises, Rachel Louise Snyder pulls back the curtain on how abuse is often misunderstood, minimized, or missed entirely—by friends, communities, and even the systems meant to protect people. Through survivor stories and reporting with advocates and law enforcement, she shows how warning signs can hide in plain sight and why leaving isn’t a simple “just walk away” moment.
 The book also points to real, practical ways prevention and intervention can work—when we stop relying on myths and start taking patterns, risk, and safety seriously. 💜
 What’s one myth about domestic violence you’ve heard that you wish people would unlearn—and why? 🗣️

School absences are a growing problem around the world, with rates in some countries nearly doubling since before COVID. 
 Attendance problems can be caused by issues inside and outside school, such as illness, mental health, family circumstances, poverty and safety. 
 Often the students who are long-term absent feel a lower sense of belonging at school, are bullied more and have worse academic outcomes.
 School attendance won't be fixed by enforcement alone. Schools also need to focus on creating environments where students feel safe, supported, and engaged in learning.

items.title: AI is moving fast. But behind all of that technology are some very basic resources: water, electricity, land and public...
items.content_text:
AI is moving fast. But behind all of that technology are some very basic resources: water, electricity, land and public infrastructure.
 And those resources are already under pressure.
 August is National Water Quality Month, which makes this a good time to talk about something that often gets lost in conversations about the AI boom: what happens to the communities where this infrastructure is being built?
 Across the South, Black communities are already dealing with aging water systems, pollution, higher energy burdens and decades of underinvestment.
 Now, Georgia and Texas are seeing data centers drive up demand for massive amounts of electricity and water. These projects can bring billions of dollars in private investment, but communities are left with important questions:
 How much water will these facilities use?
 How much electricity will they require?
 Who will pay for the infrastructure needed to support them?
 Who is getting the tax breaks?
 And what are the people who already live there getting in return?
 We’ve seen this story before.
 Black communities have too often been asked to carry the environmental and infrastructure costs of “economic development” while corporations and investors walk away with the biggest benefits.
 That’s why communities need a real seat at the table as the AI economy expands.
 The future is being built in our communities. The people who live there should have a say in what gets built, what it costs, and who benefits.
 #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #DataCenters #EnvironmentalJustice #BlackCommunities #ClimateJustice #WaterQuality #Infrastructure

items.content_text:
Parenting is one of the most important jobs, and no one should have to do it alone.
 Parents as Teachers (PAT) is a free, voluntary, evidence-based home visiting program designed to support families with young children. Recognizing that every family is unique, support is delivered directly to your home, where learning and development occur every day.
 Through regular home visits, families receive guidance on child development, parenting support, and strategies to strengthen the bond between parents and their children. Parents are acknowledged as their child's first and most important teachers, and this program is designed to enhance that role.
 Parents as Teachers aims to walk alongside families, offering support rather than directing them.
 If you are interested in the Parents as Teachers program, please call (423) 209-8298 or visit health.hamiltontn.org/…/childse…/parentsasteachers(pat).aspx.

Young people should have a say in the policies shaping their future. 
 That is why the OECD created #Youthwise, its Youth Advisory Board. The programme brings together young people from across OECD countries, giving them a platform to share their perspectives, contribute ideas and take part in international policy discussions. 
 Through meetings, workshops, consultations and high-level events, Youthwise members engage directly with OECD experts, policymakers and other stakeholders.  
 They bring valuable insights into the challenges facing their generation and help ensure that young people’s experiences are reflected in policy debates.

📚 Red Bank Residents: Free Chattanooga Public Library Cards Are Back!
 Great news! The City of Red Bank is continuing its partnership with the Chattanooga Public Library for 2026–2027, funding 200 no-cost full-access library cards for eligible Red Bank residents.
 ✨ Cards can be obtained or renewed at no cost at any of CPL’s five locations.
 With a Chattanooga Public Library card, residents can access much more than books—including:
 📖 Digital materials
 🛠️ Makerspace resources
 🎙️ Recording studio
 🎨 Library of Things
 👧 Children’s programs
 …and much more!
 The cards are available first-come, first-served, with one card per household.
 👨‍👩‍👧 Families with children: Red Bank residents with children enrolled in a Hamilton County school can sign their children up for a free HCDE library card. All Hamilton County children ages 0–5 are also eligible for a free library card.
